title: Downtown Pest walking guide: Parliament, Basilica and the Danube
description: A relaxed self-guided walk through Budapest's central Pest sights, from Parliament to St Stephen's Basilica, Vörösmarty Square and the Chain Bridge.

heroImage.alt: The Hungarian Parliament Building seen across the Danube in daylight
heroImage.creditTitle: Hungarian Parliament Building from across the Danube, 2025-01-11.jpg

intro: Downtown Pest rewards wandering. Its central streets put architectural landmarks, historic cafés and the Danube within reach of one another. This self-guided route follows a loose north-to-south line through the city centre, leaving plenty of room for cafés, interior visits and unexpected detours. It is not a timed tour.
highlights: Start at Kossuth Square for the Parliament exterior
Continue to St Stephen's Basilica and Széchenyi István Square
Finish around Vörösmarty Square and the river, or extend to the Great Market Hall

sections.title: Start at Parliament and Kossuth Square

children.text: The Hungarian Parliament building is one of Budapest's defining riverfront landmarks. Start outside on Kossuth Lajos Square, where you can appreciate the building's scale without an interior ticket. If you want a guided visit inside, arrange the correct admission separately through the official visitor service.

A little farther along the embankment, Shoes on the Danube Bank commemorates people murdered on the riverbank during the Holocaust. Visit in a quiet, respectful spirit; it is not simply another photo stop.
Check Parliament entry and security rules before your date.
Keep the memorial visit unhurried and respectful.

sections.title: Find your way towards St Stephen's Basilica

children.text: Walk into the city-centre streets and make St Stephen's Basilica your next landmark. The surrounding square is inviting even if you choose not to enter. Religious services, visitor entry and any additional areas such as lookouts may follow separate rules.
Take a little time on the surrounding streets rather than treating the route as a direct dash between monuments. The city centre is as much about its façades and corner cafés as its headline sights.

sections.title: Head towards Chain Bridge and the river

children.text: From the basilica area, continue towards Széchenyi István Square and the Chain Bridge approaches. Gresham Palace is a useful architectural landmark on the square; the bridge opens the view towards the Buda hills and the Castle District opposite.
You can cross to Buda if your day has enough time, or stay on the Pest side to continue along the river. The view back across the Danube is one of the simplest pleasures of this route.

sections.title: Choose your café stop around Vörösmarty Square

children.text: Vörösmarty Square and nearby Váci Street make an easy final city-centre cluster. The streets are popular with visitors and shoppers; a short turn into the smaller surrounding lanes offers a change of pace.

Café Gerbeaud is a historic option on the square. Its official website says there is no reservation system and guests take free tables in order of arrival, so expect to wait at busy moments, and check the current menu there rather than assuming a particular price.

sections.title: Extend the walk towards the Great Market Hall

children.text: If you still have energy, continue south towards the Great Market Hall for a different atmosphere. This takes you beyond the compact core of District V, so allow extra time and check market trading hours.
For a shorter day, end at the river and enjoy the view. Many visitors get more from a shorter walk and an unplanned pause than from squeezing in one more distant sight.
This is a suggested walking sequence, not calculated live directions.
Check accessible transport options and venue entrances individually.
Plan around confirmed admissions, not guessed opening times.

St. Stephen's Basilica took fifty-four years to build, from 1851, and is 96 metres tall. It was given the title of basilica minor in 1931. The Dohány Street Synagogue was built between 1854 and 1859 and is described as the largest synagogue in Europe, with seating for about 3,000 people; the Raoul Wallenberg Holocaust Memorial Park lies behind it, and the Heroes' Temple and the Jewish Museum belong to the same complex.

The House of Terror at Andrássy út 60 opened as a museum on 24 February 2002. It is a memorial to the victims of the fascist and communist regimes in 20th-century Hungary, in a building used by both the Arrow Cross and the ÁVH, and some displays are disturbing. Check the opening arrangements of all three before you plan the day, and allow time rather than rushing the memorials.

sections.title: Walking the Danube promenade between the bridges

children.text: The Pest riverbank has its own name, the Dunakorzó or Danube Promenade, running between the Széchenyi Chain Bridge and the Erzsébet Bridge. Gresham Palace and the Hungarian Academy of Sciences stand at its northern end; the Academy was founded in 1825, when Count István Széchenyi offered a year's income from his estate. The Chain Bridge opened in 1849 as the first permanent bridge across the Danube in Hungary, and it was closed for renovation from March 2021 to August 2023.

Farther south, Vigadó Square is home to the Vigadó concert hall, and Március 15 Square has remains of the Roman Contra-Aquincum bastion beside the Inner City Parish Church, a Romanesque basilica that served as a mosque under Ottoman rule before its Baroque remodelling. Treat this stretch as a slow detour along the water.

sections.title: Use the metro and trams to shorten the walk

children.text: You do not have to walk every leg. Metro line M1, the Millennium Underground, opened in 1896 and is described as the first electrified underground railway on the European mainland. It runs beneath Andrássy Avenue, part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing extended in 2002, and its terminus is Vörösmarty tér, with Deák Ferenc tér and Opera among the following stops.

The House of Terror and the Opera House stand on Andrássy Avenue in District VI, outside the central District V core, so link them by M1. Kossuth Square has a tram 2 stop and an M2 metro station, handy for starting or ending at Parliament. BKK publishes maps of the central network and of Andrássy út, and links its BudapestGO planner for live connections.

sections.title: Visiting memorials and churches with care

children.text: Some stops are places of worship or remembrance before they are sights. St. Stephen's Basilica is an active church, and its official site lists the church hall and the Panorama Terrace and Treasury separately, with their own visitor rules; the dome is reached by lift or 364 steps. The Dohány Street Synagogue complex includes a courtyard where more than 2,000 people who died in the Pest ghetto in 1944-45 are buried, so keep your voice low.

The Shoes on the Danube Bank, created by the sculptor Gyula Pauer and erected in 2005, has sixty pairs of iron shoes honouring about 23,500 people shot into the Danube during the Arrow Cross terror, roughly 20,000 of them Jews. At the House of Terror, some historians criticise how the museum presents Hungary's role, so read its account alongside other sources.

faqs.question: Can I walk between the main Downtown Pest sights?
faqs.answer: Yes, the central landmarks in this guide lend themselves to a walking visit. Adapt the length to your pace and mobility needs.

faqs.question: Do I need to buy tickets for the whole route?
faqs.answer: No. The public streets and riverfront are open to explore without a tour ticket. Individual interiors and venues have separate admission arrangements.

faqs.question: Is the Jewish Quarter part of this walk?
faqs.answer: Only in part. The historic Jewish quarter of Pest lies in District VII, where the Dohány Street Synagogue stands; the main route concentrates on the central Pest area, particularly District V, so treat the synagogue as a short detour.

faqs.question: How do I get from Vörösmarty Square to Andrássy Avenue?
faqs.answer: Metro line M1 starts at Vörösmarty tér and runs beneath Andrássy Avenue, with stops including Deák Ferenc tér and Opera. Check BKK for current service.

faqs.question: Can I go up St. Stephen's Basilica for the view?
faqs.answer: The basilica's official site lists a Panorama Terrace separately from the church hall, and the dome can be reached by lift or 364 steps. Check the site first.

faqs.question: Is the Chain Bridge good to walk across?
faqs.answer: It reopened in 2023 after renovation and is described as car-free, so it suits a walk with views of Parliament and the Buda hills. Check BKK for closures.

title: Budapest food and markets: first-time guide to cafés and local flavours
description: Discover the Great Market Hall, famous Budapest cafés, classic Hungarian dishes and practical tips for a food-focused city break.

heroImage.alt: Shoppers walking between stalls under the iron roof of the Great Market Hall
heroImage.caption: Budapest city panorama — not a photograph of the food venues in this article.

intro: A good Budapest food day does not need a perfect checklist. Try a market, make time for a café and order a dish that interests you. This guide focuses on a small number of documented venues already in our directory, plus useful pointers for discovering Hungarian flavours at your own pace. It is not a restaurant ranking or a personal tasting review.
highlights: Go to the Great Market Hall to browse food stalls and ingredients
Consider Café Gerbeaud and New York Café for very different historic interiors
Check menu prices, allergens and reservations with each venue

sections.title: Start with the Great Market Hall

children.text: The Great Market Hall is an easy introduction to Budapest's market culture. Browse before buying and take time to compare stalls. Traditional ingredients, everyday produce and food-to-go can share the same building, but traders and selections change.

Market hours may differ from typical restaurant hours and can change around holidays. Verify the official opening information for your visit; avoid planning a final-day market stop around a guessed schedule.

sections.title: A café stop near Vörösmarty Square

children.text: Café Gerbeaud is a well-known historic café in central Pest. Its location makes it a convenient addition to a stroll around Vörösmarty Square and Váci Street.
The atmosphere may be a reason to visit as much as the menu. Check the current menu and booking arrangements directly, and decide whether the experience fits your budget and appetite.

sections.title: The theatrical interiors of New York Café

children.text: New York Café offers an ornate setting away from the compact District V core. It works best as a deliberate stop in a wider city walk rather than an assumed quick detour from the river.
Popular historic cafés may have waits or their own admission and reservation policies. Always verify the current arrangements with the venue instead of relying on old travel videos.

sections.title: What to look for on a Hungarian menu

children.text: Gulyás is a familiar starting point, alongside paprika-seasoned dishes, lángos and pastries such as rétes. These names describe broad traditions, not a promise that every café or stall will serve them in the same way.
If you have food allergies or other dietary requirements, ask the venue about the specific preparation and ingredients. Translations and menus can be incomplete.

sections.title: Leave room for your own discoveries

children.text: A market breakfast, riverside walk and afternoon coffee often make more sense than travelling across the city for three famous venues in one day. Choose stops close to where you already plan to be.
Treat this guide as an editorial starting point. GoToBudapest currently has three detailed food-and-market attraction entries, and those are not an exhaustive account of Budapest dining.

Gulyás is the dish visitors most often get wrong. In Hungary it is a soup, even though English-language menus often call it a stew. It is described as a one-pot dish seasoned with paprika, usually built on beef or mutton with onion, caraway, potatoes, carrots and small pinched noodles called csipetke. The word means cattle herder, which points to its origin on the plains. Pörkölt is its thicker cousin: a stew of meat, onion and sweet paprika that can be made with chicken, pork or other meat, and paprikás is the version finished with sour cream. If you want the soup, ask for gulyásleves; if you want a stew on rice or with dumplings, look for pörkölt or paprikás.

Lángos is fried yeast dough, traditionally eaten warm, with toppings such as sour cream, grated cheese, sausage, bacon or garlic. It began as a way of using leftover bread dough and is sold at markets, fairs and fast-food counters. Kürtőskalács, the chimney cake, is a strip of sweet yeast dough wound around a spit, rolled in sugar and roasted over charcoal until the sugar forms a crisp caramel crust; it is associated with the Székely people of Transylvania, and the first written record dates from 1679. Dobos torte, a sponge cake layered with chocolate buttercream under a hard caramel top, was introduced by the Budapest delicatessen owner József C. Dobos at the 1885 national exhibition.

Two more names to know are túrós csusza, egg noodles with túró (a fresh curd cheese, similar to quark), served savoury with bacon or sweet with sugar, and halászlé, a hot paprika fish soup whose recipe varies between the Danube and Tisza river regions. Rétes, the strudel, is the traditional pastry. Menus and recipes differ from place to place, so treat these descriptions as a guide to what to expect, not a rulebook.
Gulyás is a soup; pörkölt is a thicker stew; paprikás adds sour cream.
Lángos and kürtőskalács are snacks to share while walking.
Ask staff how a dish is prepared if you have a food allergy.

sections.title: How a Hungarian meal works, and what to drink

children.text: Traditionally, lunch is the main meal of the day and may have several courses: soup first, then a main dish, then dessert. Dinner is described as less important, and there is no single typical Hungarian dinner. Traditional cooking rests on meat, seasonal vegetables, fruit, bread and dairy, with chicken, pork and beef the everyday meats. Paprika is the defining spice, and both sweet and hot varieties are common, so a Hungarian menu is not automatically fiery.

Hungary has several wine regions. Tokaj in the north-east is the best known, famous for the sweet Tokaji aszú, made from individually picked grapes affected by noble rot, and also for dry Furmint; the Tokaj wine region was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape in 2002. Eger is associated with the red blend Egri Bikavér, and Etyek-Buda, close to Budapest, is known for fresh white wines. Ask a wine bar or restaurant for a glass of a region you have not tried.

Pálinka is a fruit brandy, usually from plums, apricots, apples, pears or cherries. Under Hungary's 2008 law only a spirit made from Hungarian-grown fruit and distilled and bottled in Hungary may carry the name, and it has had EU protected status since 2004. Unicum is a bitter herbal liqueur made by the Zwack company from a secret blend of herbs and aged in oak casks; it is usually taken as a digestif and is described as an acquired taste. Drink both slowly: they are strong spirits, not table wines.

sections.title: The Great Market Hall and other markets

children.text: The Great Market Hall at Fővám tér is Budapest's largest and oldest indoor market. It was designed by Samu Pecz and opened on 15 February 1897, and its roof is covered in coloured Zsolnay tiles. Inside, the ground floor is mostly produce, meat, pastries, spices and spirits, an upper level holds food stalls and souvenirs, and the basement has fish and pickled vegetables. The hall was badly damaged in the Second World War, and a renovation begun in 1991 led to its reopening in 1997. Walk the whole hall before you buy: prices and quality differ from stall to stall.

Other markets give a more local picture. The Rákóczi tér Market Hall in District VIII was one of the big halls of the 1890s. It was destroyed by fire in 1988 and rebuilt, reopening in 1991; it is a working neighbourhood market, mostly meat and groceries. The Lehel Market Hall in District XIII at Váci út, designed to look like a ship, is described by local-food writers as a neighbourhood hall for fresh produce, cheese, sausages and lángos. The Fény utca market, on the Buda side near Széll Kálmán tér, is described as a semi-open-air, multi-storey market with produce, baked goods, wine and seasonal events.

Sources disagree on details such as the opening year of the Rákóczi tér hall, which is given as 1894 in some places (when building began) and 1897 elsewhere, and on traders and hours, which change. Check each market's current arrangements before a special trip, and note that market halls are working shops first and sightseeing stops second.

sections.title: Coffee houses and pastry, with their history

children.text: Café Gerbeaud on Vörösmarty tér has a long story. Henrik Kugler founded the business in 1858 and moved it to what is now Vörösmarty tér in 1870. He invited the confectioner Émile Gerbeaud to Budapest in 1884, and Gerbeaud eventually took over the business and kept the name. Today its own website highlights its pastry selection, its coffee blend and classic sweets such as cognac sour cherries and cat's tongues.

The New York Café on Erzsébet körút opened on 23 October 1894 on the ground floor of a New York insurance company building, and was long a meeting place for Hungarian writers and poets. After the Second World War the café was renamed Hungaria in 1954 and regained its original name in 1989. The building was later restored and reopened as a hotel with the café inside. Because it is both a historic interior and a popular stop, allow extra time and read the venue's own page for seating and reservation rules.

A practical approach: choose one historic café for atmosphere and eat the rest of your pastry at neighbourhood confectioners, where the focus is on the cake itself. Order a Dobos torte, a rétes or a slice of whatever the display case recommends, and let the coffee house be a rest from sightseeing rather than a race through the sights.

Traditional Hungarian cuisine is built on meat, so vegetarians may find the classic menu limited, and traditional sweets often contain a lot of egg and dairy. Dedicated vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free and kosher kitchens exist in Budapest, especially in the central districts and in Erzsébetváros, the old Jewish Quarter, where a glatt kosher Hungarian-Jewish restaurant is listed by one city directory. On menus, look for the words vegán, gluténmentes and kóser. Listings of such places are compiled by third parties and details differ, so confirm certification, kitchen practice and halal or kosher status directly with the venue.

If you would like help with orientation, food experiences come in several types. Guided culinary and wine walks, sommelier-led wine tastings and visits to food markets are all offered by local companies, and some multi-day programmes include baking Hungarian holiday desserts. Read what each experience actually covers before choosing, and remember that none of these is needed: a market stroll and a coffee-house stop already give you a fair taste of the city.

faqs.question: Is this a list of the best restaurants in Budapest?
faqs.answer: No. It is a curated introduction to markets and historic cafés, not a quality ranking or first-hand review of every venue.

faqs.question: Do I need a booking for a famous café?
faqs.answer: Reservation rules vary by venue and date. Use the official venue site for current details.

faqs.question: Can I rely on fixed food prices in travel guides?
faqs.answer: No. Check the venue's current menu and any service charges before ordering.

faqs.question: Is gulyás in Budapest a soup or a stew?
faqs.answer: In Hungary gulyás is a paprika-flavoured soup, usually made with beef, onion, potatoes and small noodles. The thicker dish that English speakers often call goulash is closer to pörkölt, so check the menu wording if you want a stew.

faqs.question: What are Hungarian pálinka and Unicum?
faqs.answer: Pálinka is a Hungarian fruit brandy, often from plums, apricots or pears, and the name is legally protected. Unicum is a bitter herbal liqueur made by the Zwack company and usually drunk as a digestif. Both are strong, so sip slowly.

faqs.question: Is Budapest food hard for vegetarians?
faqs.answer: Traditional Hungarian cooking is meat-heavy, so classic menus can be limited for vegetarians. Dedicated vegetarian and vegan restaurants exist, and many places can adapt, but ask staff about ingredients and check the venue's own menu.

faqs.question: Which markets can I visit besides the Great Market Hall?
faqs.answer: Local-food writers and market sources mention the Rákóczi tér Market Hall in District VIII, the Lehel Market Hall in District XIII and the Fény utca market near Széll Kálmán tér. Hours and traders change, so check current details before going.
